excerpt_original: Kader Attia reveals curatorial vision for seventh Kochi-Muziris Biennale, Trellis Art Fund names 2026 Stepping Stone grantees, Elie Khouri to open private art foundation in Dubai, and more. The Editors

Kader Attia Unveils Curatorial Framework for 2027 Kochi-Muziris Biennale

Algerian French artist and curator Kader Attia has revealed that the seventh Kochi-Muziris Biennale will center on “the relationship between dreams, memory, and repair.” Attia, who was appointed earlier this year to helm the forthcoming exhibition, is known for exploring the concept of repair in his own artistic practice. His curatorial vision foregrounds the unpredictability of dreams as a counter to the formulaic logic of AI, which is increasingly mediating the human condition. In a statement, Attia remarked, “Our subjectivity is fragmented, like the internet, . . . yet there we are tracked by the algorithm. Exhibitions are important because they produce emotions, activating new traces in our minds.” He added that “dreams repair us, like art… and the biennale, as well as Kerala, will give us the space-time to reclaim our sovereignty over our dreams.” The seventh edition is slated to take place from December 12, 2027 to March 31, 2028 across several sites in the port city of Kochi.

Trellis Art Fund Announces 2026 Stepping Stone Grantees

The New York-based nonprofit Trellis Art Fund has announced the recipients of its 2026 Stepping Stone cohort, an initiative dedicated to supporting up-and-coming artists with “promising artistic practices.” Among the 20 grantees in this year’s roster are Korean American artist Rachel Youn , known for her kinetic plant-machine installations; Hong Kong Canadian sculptor Jes Fan, whose sculptures and videos probe themes of queerness and diasporic identity; Japanese American visual artist and 2019 Guggenheim fellow Carrie Yamaoka, known for engaging with questions of perception and materiality across various media; California-based ceramicist Cathy Lu, who draws on traditional Chinese iconography to interrogate culture and belonging; the New York-based collective CFGNY (comprising artists Daniel Chew, Ten Izu, and Tin Nguyen), whose work addresses racial politics through textiles and fashion; and the Palestinian duo Basel Abbas and Ruanne Abou-Rahme, whose films, performances, and audiovisual installations reflect on collective memory, grief, and Palestinian resistance. Each grantee will receive an unrestricted fund of USD 40,000 over a two-year period to support their practices.

Elie Khouri Art Foundation to Open in Dubai in 2028

French Lebanese collector and philanthropist Elie Khouri is set to open the Elie Khouri Art Foundation (EKAF) in late 2028 in Dubai’s Jumeirah 1 district. The building—an existing coastal villa to be redesigned by South African architect Sumayya Vally and her practice Counterspace—will feature learning spaces, pavilions, a garden, and galleries housing works by more than 300 artists from Khouri’s holdings. Drawing from the collection, EKAF’s exhibitions will spotlight practitioners from the UAE and beyond, further presenting institutional loans, collaborations, and educational programs under the direction of Caroline Louca, formerly managing director of Christie’s Middle East. Though Khouri, who has lived in Dubai since the 1990s, founded EKAF in 2021, plans for a permanent venue only started this year. In a statement, he said: “Art belongs in everyday life, not apart from it. My foundation will be a home for contemporary art, open to everyone. A place to inspire, challenge, and spark dialogue. Above all, I want to give something lasting back to Dubai and the wider UAE, a country that has given me so much, by helping build a cultural legacy for generations to come.”

MCA Australia Appoints Sophie O’Brien as Senior Curator, Exhibitions

Sydney’s Museum of Contemporary Art Australia (MCA) has appointed curator and writer Sophie O’Brien as its new senior curator of exhibitions, succeeding Jane Devery, who concluded her four-year tenure in August. O’Brien brings more than two decades of experience, joining MCA from the Bundanon Art Museum in Illaroo, where she served as head of curatorial and learning for over six years. Previously, she was senior curator at the Serpentine Galleries in London, curator of contemporary British art at Tate Britain, and head of exhibitions and collections at the Govett-Brewster Art Gallery in Aotearoa, New Zealand. Aside from holding curatorial positions at Artspace Sydney and the Art Gallery of Western Australia, she also led the teams for the Australian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale (2005–07) and the 14th Biennale of Sydney (2005). At MCA, O’Brien will oversee the research and development of the institution’s exhibition program. In a press release, MCA director Suzanne Cotter noted, “[O’Brien’s] international perspective, leadership, and commitment to artistic excellence will be invaluable as we continue to build on [our] reputation as Australia’s leading contemporary art museum.”
SHEIKHA NAWAR AL QASSIMI , vice president of the Sharjah Art Foundation (SAF) with winner
ARIEF BUDIMAN , jury members, and the SAF film team at the award ceremony for Sharjah Film Platform 9, Sharjah, 2026. Courtesy SAF.

The Sharjah Art Foundation (SAF) has announced the 2026 winners of its Sharjah Film Platform. Now in its ninth edition, the festival spotlights independent filmmakers from the UAE and abroad, awarding recipients across four categories. Rania Rafei’s The Day of Wrath: Tales from Tripoli (2026), which chronicles the fraught history of Lebanon’s second-largest city through personal and collective memory, clinched Best Documentary Feature Film. Yogyakarta-based filmmaker Arief Budiman won Best Documentary Short Film for Shadow of Sakura (2025), which delves into the violent Japanese occupation of Indonesia. Best Fiction Feature Film went to South African screenwriter and director Zamo Mkhwanazi for Uhlanjululo (Laundry) (2025), which examines the harrowing legacy of apartheid, while Asim Abdulaziz earned Best Fiction Short Film for I Broke a Vase (2026), a haunting reflection on the Yemeni civil war through the eyes of a journalist. Additionally, David Bim received a special mention in the Documentary Feature category for Al Oeste, En Zapata (To the West, in Zapata) (2025), a black-and-white film portraying a Cuban family’s struggles during the Covid-19 pandemic. In a press release, SAF noted that the winning works “reflect the richness of contemporary independent cinema and its capacity to engage with social, cultural, and political questions.”
